metadata.title: Quantum computing for ﬁnance: overview and prospects

problem_domains.description: Determining how to construct and dynamically adjust an optimal portfolio over time, balancing return, risk, and transaction costs under constraints.
problem_domains.quote:
Dynamic Portfolio Selection is an example of optimiza-
tion: given a selection of assets i, withi∈ [1,n ], the goal
is to maximize the ﬁnal proﬁts at time t = T . Let xi,t
be the amount of money we choose invest in asset i at
timet∈ [0,T−1], and let Ri,t+1 be the returns resulting
from this decision.
problem_domains.location: Page 2, Section II.B Relevant approaches in quantitative ﬁnance

problem_domains.problem: optimal trading trajectory (dynamic portfolio optimization with costs and impact)
problem_domains.description: Finding the optimal trajectory in portfolio space over multiple periods while accounting for transaction costs and market impact under holding constraints.
problem_domains.quote:
Let us consider the problem of dynamic portfolio op-
timization, described in Sec. II B. Our aim is to ﬁnd the
optimal trajectory in the portfolio space, while taking
into account transaction costs and market impact.
problem_domains.location: Page 5, Section III.A Optimal trading trajectory

problem_domains.description: Identifying the most profitable arbitrage cycle across assets and markets, which is NP-Hard when searching for the optimal opportunity.
problem_domains.quote:
The concept of arbitrage is the idea of making proﬁt
from diﬀering prices in the same asset in diﬀerent mar-
kets. ... The problem of determining the optimal arbi-
trage opportunity, however, is NP-Hard.
problem_domains.location: Page 6, Section III.B Optimal arbitrage opportunities

problem_domains.description: Estimating the level of risk associated with a loan by classifying borrowers as high or low risk based on their characteristics.
problem_domains.quote:
It is essential for banks and other ﬁnancial institutions
which specialize in lending money to estimate the level of
risk associated with a loan, i.e: if the borrower is likely
to default on his payments. This is credit scoring: before
granting a loan, banks consider the borrower’s income,
age, ﬁnancial history, collateral, ... to identify them as a
high risk or low risk customer.
problem_domains.location: Page 6, Section III.C Optimal feature selection in credit scoring

problem_domains.problem: optimal feature selection in credit scoring
problem_domains.description: Selecting the subset of borrower features that are most informative and least redundant for predicting creditworthiness, under data and computational constraints.
problem_domains.quote:
we want to determine which data on past appli-
cants can provide useful information in determining the
creditworthiness of new applicants. This problem arises
when some of the data is irrelevant or weakly correlated
to the output, when we do not have access to all the data,
and when performing credit scoring by using all the data
is too computationally expensive.
problem_domains.location: Page 6–7, Section III.C Optimal feature selection in credit scoring

problem_domains.description: Predicting future behavior of assets and markets, including stock prices, using patterns in past data.
problem_domains.quote:
Among the huge variety of prob-
lems ﬁnance attempts to address, we ﬁnd stock markets
prediction, portfolio optimization, and fraud detection.
problem_domains.location: Page 1, Introduction

problem_domains.description: Detecting anomalous or fraudulent transactions or customers by identifying data points that are hard to classify.
problem_domains.quote:
Data classiﬁcation algorithms are also
used for outlier detection, where we identify points which
are diﬃcult to correctly attribute to a class. This type
of process is essential for fraud detection [55].
problem_domains.location: Page 7, Section IV.A Data classiﬁcation

problem_domains.description: Forecasting demand (e.g., product sales) and other economic quantities by learning numeric relationships between multiple weak indicators.
problem_domains.quote:
Another common ﬁnancial problem is known as supply
chain management, which is the art of meeting customer
demand while avoiding unwanted stock. As with classiﬁ-
cation algorithms, it can be essential to take into account
a number of weak indicators when dealing with this type
of problem.
problem_domains.location: Page 7–8, Section IV.B Regression

problem_domains.description: Valuing options and other derivatives whose payoffs depend in complex ways on underlying assets, often requiring Monte Carlo simulation.
problem_domains.quote:
Options’ pay-
oﬀs depend on the value of other assets (hence the name
of derivatives) in complex ways. ... in general
requires numerical simulation methods (such as Monte
Carlo).
problem_domains.location: Page 2, Section II.A Some core problems in ﬁnance

problem_domains.description: Estimating risk of assets and portfolios, including distributions of returns and risk measures, often via Monte Carlo.
problem_domains.quote:
This randomness is a
source of risk which can be extremely diﬃcult to esti-
mate. This is for instance the case of options, which
are a special case of derivative security.
problem_domains.location: Page 2, Section II.A Some core problems in ﬁnance

problem_domains.problem: Monte Carlo-based estimation of risk and return
problem_domains.description: Using Monte Carlo simulations to estimate expected returns and their distributions for assets and portfolios.
problem_domains.quote:
Monte Carlo methods can usually be implemented eﬃ-
ciently, but require many runs to provide an accurate
estimation of the expected return and its distribution.
problem_domains.location: Page 3, Section II.B Relevant approaches in quantitative ﬁnance

problem_domains.description: Identifying patterns in past financial data for tasks like economic forecasting, voice/facial recognition analogues, and other predictive analytics.
problem_domains.quote:
Another way to approach ﬁnancial problems is to
search for patterns in past data. This is a natural way to
consider economic forecasting problems, an area where
machine learning methods have proved to be extremely
successful.
problem_domains.location: Page 1–2, Introduction

problem_domains.problem: principal component analysis for interest rate and portfolio risk
problem_domains.description: Extracting principal components of large covariance matrices (e.g., interest rate paths, stock price changes) to understand trends and estimate risk in portfolios.
problem_domains.quote:
In portfolio optimization, which we discussed in Sec.
II B, it is essential to have a global vision of interest rates
paths, even when dealing with hundreds of swap instru-
ments [71]. A standard tool for doing this is a machine
learning algorithm known as principal component analy-
sis (PCA).
problem_domains.location: Page 8, Section IV.C Principal component analysis

problem_domains.description: Broad class of optimization problems in finance, including which assets to include in a portfolio and how composition should change with the market.
problem_domains.quote:
Which assets should be
included in an optimum
portfolio? How should the
composition of the portfolio
change according to what
happens in the market?
Optimization models
problem_domains.location: Page 2, Table I

problem_domains.problem: detecting opportunities in different assets in the market
problem_domains.description: Identifying profitable trading opportunities across assets using machine learning, including neural networks and deep learning.
problem_domains.quote:
How to detect opportunities
in the diﬀerent assets in the
market, and take proﬁt by
trading with them?
Machine learning methods,
including neural networks
and deep learning
problem_domains.location: Page 2, Table I

problem_domains.problem: estimating risk and return of a portfolio or company
problem_domains.description: Estimating risk and return metrics for portfolios or companies using Monte Carlo-based methods.
problem_domains.quote:
How to estimate the risk
and return of a portfolio, or
even a company?
Monte Carlo-based methods
problem_domains.location: Page 2, Table I

problem_domains.problem: predicting markets and analyzing credit risk
problem_domains.description: Use of neural networks to predict financial markets and assess credit risk.
problem_domains.quote: Neural networks have proved extremely successful at predicting markets and analyzing credit risk [72, 73].
problem_domains.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 1

problem_domains.description: Application of neural networks to prediction of financial time series.
problem_domains.quote: These properties have made neural networks essential for, e.g., ﬁnancial time-series prediction [74, 75].
problem_domains.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 1

problem_domains.description: Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations of stock markets that can take a long time to run.
problem_domains.quote: This is the case for stock market simulations, for instance, which are rou- tinely day-long simulations.
problem_domains.location: Page 9, Section V. QUANTUM AMPLITUDE ESTIMATION AND MONTE CARLO, paragraph discussing Eq. (8)

problem_domains.problem: portfolio evaluation, personal finance planning, risk evaluation, and derivatives pricing
problem_domains.description: Use of Monte Carlo methods in finance to simulate uncertainties affecting financial objects for various evaluation and pricing tasks.
problem_domains.quote: In ﬁnance, the stochastic approach is typically used to simulate the eﬀect of uncertainties aﬀecting the ﬁnancial object in question, which could be a stock, a portfolio, or an option. This makes Monte Carlo methods applicable to portfolio evaluation, personal ﬁnance planning, risk evaluation, and derivatives pricing [12].
problem_domains.location: Page 9, Section V. QUANTUM AMPLITUDE ESTIMATION AND MONTE CARLO, introductory paragraphs

problem_domains.description: Determining a fair price for derivatives whose payoff depends on stochastic future asset price trajectories.
problem_domains.quote: Brokers must know how to assign a fair price to the derivatives from the state of the market. This is the pricing problem.
problem_domains.location: Page 10, Section V.A. Pricing of ﬁnancial derivatives, paragraph 1

problem_domains.problem: pricing of a European call option and Asian options
problem_domains.description: Specific derivative pricing tasks for European call and Asian options.
problem_domains.quote: Rebentrost et al. also discuss how their method can be applied to the pric- ing of a European call option and to Asian options [11].
problem_domains.location: Page 10, Section V.A. Pricing of ﬁnancial derivatives, paragraph 2

problem_domains.problem: risk analysis via Value at Risk (VaR) and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR)
problem_domains.description: Quantifying portfolio risk using VaR and CVaR, typically estimated via Monte Carlo sampling.
problem_domains.quote:
Financial institutions need to be able to accurately manage and compute risk, which we introduced in Sec. II A. One way to mathematically quantify the risk is through the Value at Risk (VaR) function, which mea- sures the distribution of losses of a portfolio. ... Another use- ful risk estimation tool is the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), which measures the expected loss of a portfolio for losses greater than VaR.
Typically in quantitative ﬁnance, VaR and CVaR are estimated using Monte Carlo sampling of the relevant probability distribution.
problem_domains.location: Page 10, Section V.B. Risk analysis, paragraphs 1–2

solution_approaches.approach: quantum annealing for portfolio optimization / optimal trading trajectory
solution_approaches.description: Maps the discrete multi-period dynamic portfolio optimization problem with transaction costs and impact into a QUBO and solves it on a D-Wave quantum annealer.
solution_approaches.quote:
It was suggested in Ref. [48] that the discrete multi-
period version of this problem was amenable to quan-
tum annealers. This idea was implemented on a D-Wave
quantum processor in Ref. [43].
solution_approaches.location: Page 5–6, Section III.A Optimal trading trajectory

solution_approaches.approach: quantum annealing for optimal arbitrage opportunities
solution_approaches.description: Formulates the search for the most profitable arbitrage cycle as a QUBO problem and solves it using a D-Wave quantum annealer.
solution_approaches.quote:
Written in this way, the problem has been boiled
down to a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization
(QUBO) problem, which is amenable to quantum an-
nealers. These results were implemented on the D-Wave
2X quantum annealer, for a small-size example with ﬁve
assets.
solution_approaches.location: Page 6, Section III.B Optimal arbitrage opportunities

solution_approaches.approach: quantum annealing for optimal feature selection in credit scoring
solution_approaches.description: Encodes the feature selection problem for credit scoring into a QUBO cost function and optimizes it using a quantum annealer via the 1QBit SDK.
solution_approaches.quote:
In this form, Eq. (7) can be optimized by a quantum
annealer. This was implemented as a proof-of-principle
on the 1QBit SDK toolkit [50].
solution_approaches.location: Page 7, Section III.C Optimal feature selection in credit scoring

solution_approaches.approach: quantum optimization / adiabatic quantum computation
solution_approaches.description: Uses adiabatic quantum computation, implemented via quantum annealing, to find ground states of Hamiltonians encoding financial optimization cost functions.
solution_approaches.quote:
First, we must
map the optimization problem to the physical problem
of ﬁnding the ground state of a Hamiltonian HP , which
encodes the cost function to be minimized. ... We then adiabatically deform H0 toHP over
a long time T .
solution_approaches.location: Page 5, Section III Quantum Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)
solution_approaches.description: Applies QAOA to find good approximate solutions to financial optimization problems in polynomial time.
solution_approaches.quote:
Alternatively, the Quantum
Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) ﬁnds a
“good solution” (i.e: one with a minimum quality) to
an optimization problem in a polynomial time [21].
solution_approaches.location: Page 4, Section II.D The case for quantum computing in ﬁnance

solution_approaches.approach: quantum machine learning for pattern recognition and forecasting
solution_approaches.description: Uses quantum versions of machine learning algorithms, including deep learning-related subroutines, to search for patterns in financial data more efficiently.
solution_approaches.quote:
In recent years, there has
been an impressive eﬀort to develop quantum machine
learning algorithms [8], which many hope will provide
the tools to satisfy our growing data requirements.
solution_approaches.location: Page 1–2, Introduction

solution_approaches.approach: quantum data classification (swap-test-based and related methods)
solution_approaches.description: Encodes financial data points as quantum states and uses swap tests and related quantum routines to perform classification tasks such as credit scoring and fraud detection.
solution_approaches.quote:
A¨ ımeur, Brassard and Gambs pioneered the idea of re-
casting this problem on a quantum computer by express-
ing each data point as a quantum state [56]. They build
upon a proposal by Buhrman et al. [57], to eﬃciently
estimate the classical distance |⟨a|b⟩| between states|a⟩,
|b⟩ by repeatedly performing swap tests.
solution_approaches.location: Page 7, Section IV.A Data classiﬁcation

solution_approaches.approach: quantum support vector machine
solution_approaches.description: Implements support vector machines on a quantum computer with operations scaling polynomially in log N, enabling faster classification for financial tasks.
solution_approaches.quote:
There exist a number of pro-
posals to implement support vector machines on a quan-
tum computer [23, 59]. These have attracted a lot of
attention because the operations necessary to construct
the hyperplane and assign a class to a new vector scale
polynomially in log N, where N is the dimension of the
vector space.
solution_approaches.location: Page 7, Section IV.A Data classiﬁcation

solution_approaches.approach: HHL-based quantum regression (least-squares)
solution_approaches.description: Uses the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd linear systems algorithm to perform least-squares regression exponentially faster, applicable to forecasting problems.
solution_approaches.quote:
There exists, however, a powerful linear algebra tool-
box which allows us to diagonalize matrices on quantum
computers exponentially faster than on classical comput-
ers [32]. The idea of applying this algorithm to per-
form regression on a quantum computer was pioneered by
Wiebe, Braun, and Lloyd.
solution_approaches.location: Page 8, Section IV.B Regression

solution_approaches.approach: quantum Gaussian process regression
solution_approaches.description: Applies quantum linear algebra techniques to implement Gaussian process regression with exponential speedup.
solution_approaches.quote:
A method for running an altogether diﬀerent regres-
sion algorithm, known as Gaussian process regression,
was suggested in Ref. [69]. This work also relies on the
linear algebra toolbox provided by Ref. [32] to claim an
exponential speedup relative to classical algorithms.
solution_approaches.location: Page 8, Section IV.B Regression

solution_approaches.approach: quantum state-encoded regression for direct prediction
solution_approaches.description: Encodes the regression model into a quantum state and uses it directly to make predictions on new inputs, avoiding expensive tomography.
solution_approaches.quote:
Schuld,
Sinayskiy, and Petruccione circumvent this problem en-
tirely by encoding their regression model into a quantum
state, which is then used to perform predictions on new
inputs directly [70].
solution_approaches.location: Page 8, Section IV.B Regression

solution_approaches.approach: quantum principal component analysis (quantum PCA)
solution_approaches.description: Uses quantum algorithms to find principal components of large covariance/correlation matrices with exponential speedup, enabling large-scale PCA for portfolios.
solution_approaches.quote:
It was recently shown that a version of this algorithm,
the quantum-PCA algorithm, could be run exponentially
faster on a quantum processor [22]. Speciﬁcally, this
algorithm ﬁnds approximations to the principal compo-
nents of a correlation matrix, with a computational cost
ofO((logN)2) (both in computational and query com-
plexities).
solution_approaches.location: Page 8, Section IV.C Principal component analysis

solution_approaches.approach: quantum amplitude estimation for Monte Carlo
solution_approaches.description: Uses quantum amplitude estimation to achieve a quadratic speedup in Monte Carlo sampling, impacting derivative pricing and risk analysis.
solution_approaches.quote:
Finally, we consider quantum amplitude estimation,
and how it can result in a quantum speed-up for Monte Carlo sampling. This has direct applications
to many current ﬁnancial methods, including pricing of derivatives and risk analysis.
solution_approaches.location: Page 1, Abstract

solution_approaches.approach: Grover-based quantum Monte Carlo
solution_approaches.description: Adapts Grover’s algorithm to implement Monte Carlo methods with quadratic speedup.
solution_approaches.quote:
This algorithm can be adapted to solve optimization
problems, such as ﬁnding a Minimum Spanning Tree [19],
maximizing ﬂow-like variables [20], and implementing
Monte Carlo methods [9].
solution_approaches.location: Page 4, Section II.D The case for quantum computing in ﬁnance

solution_approaches.approach: quantum Boltzmann machines and other QML subroutines
solution_approaches.description: Employs quantum versions of Boltzmann machines, PCA, SVM, and reinforcement learning with various speedups for machine learning tasks in finance.
solution_approaches.quote:

solution_approaches.approach: training neural networks using a quantum annealer
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum annealing hardware such as D-Wave or Rigetti to reduce the computational cost of training neural networks.
solution_approaches.quote: This overhead could be signiﬁcantly reduced by training the neural network using a quantum an- nealer, such as the D-Wave or the Rigetti machines.
solution_approaches.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 2

solution_approaches.approach: Boltzmann machine trained using present day D-Wave quantum computer
solution_approaches.description: Demonstration that a Boltzmann machine can be efficiently trained on existing D-Wave hardware.
solution_approaches.quote: In an early implementation of this idea, Ref. [79] have shown that a Boltzmann machine could be eﬃciently trained using present day D-Wave quantum computer.
solution_approaches.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 3

solution_approaches.approach: quantum PCA methods to implement iterative gradient descent
solution_approaches.description: Use quantum principal component analysis to exponentially speed up neural network training via gradient descent.
solution_approaches.quote: Alternatively, the training process could be sped-up exponentially (compared to classical training methods) by using quantum PCA methods to implement iterative gradient descent methods for network training [22].
solution_approaches.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 5

solution_approaches.approach: quantum perceptron models
solution_approaches.description: Fully quantum neural network algorithms based on quantum perceptrons.
solution_approaches.quote: Early suggestions in this ﬁeld include quantum perceptron models [26] and quantum hidden Markov models [80].
solution_approaches.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 7

solution_approaches.approach: quantum hidden Markov models
solution_approaches.description: Quantum generalizations of hidden Markov models promising richer dynamical processes for forecasting.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum hidden Markov models, being a generalization of their classical counterparts, promise richer dynamical processes.
solution_approaches.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 7

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) and quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo
solution_approaches.description: Use QAE to obtain a quadratic speed-up in Monte Carlo estimation of expectation values.
solution_approaches.quote: In particular, it can be used to obtain a quadratic speed-up in the calculation of expec- tation values by Monte Carlo sampling.
solution_approaches.location: Page 9, Section V. QUANTUM AMPLITUDE ESTIMATION AND MONTE CARLO, paragraph on QAE

solution_approaches.approach: Montanaro’s quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods
solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithm that estimates means with O(σ/ϵ) samples instead of O(σ²/ϵ²) using QAE.
solution_approaches.quote: Building upon this result, Montanaro showed that Monte Carlo simulations can run on a quantum com- puter, obtaining the same accuracy as predicted by Eq. (8) but with almost quadratically less samples k [10]. Speciﬁcally, Montanaro’s algorithm requires onlyO(σ/ϵ) samples (up to polylogarithmic factors) to estimate µ with 99% success probability.
solution_approaches.location: Page 10, Section V. QUANTUM AMPLITUDE ESTIMATION AND MONTE CARLO, paragraph after QAE description

solution_approaches.approach: quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo for pricing financial derivatives
solution_approaches.description: Design a quantum operator with the derivative’s payoff distribution and use Montanaro’s method to estimate its expectation value.
solution_approaches.quote: Building upon Montanaro’s work, Rebentrost, Gupt, and Bromley suggested using quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo to obtain a quadratic speedup in pricing ﬁ- nancial derivatives [11]. The idea is to design a quantum operator which has the same probability distribution as the ﬁnancial derivative, and apply the method from Ref. [10] to estimate its expectation value.
solution_approaches.location: Page 10, Section V.A. Pricing of ﬁnancial derivatives, paragraph 2

solution_approaches.approach: quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo for VaR and CVaR via QAE and tailored oracle
solution_approaches.description: Apply QAE with a tailored oracle to efficiently estimate VaR and CVaR with quadratic speedup.
solution_approaches.quote: Woerner and Egger pioneered the idea of adapting the core principles of quantum- accelerated Monte Carlo to eﬃciently estimate these vari- ables [81]. Speciﬁcally, by applying the QAE algorithm, which called a tailored oracle function, they were able to determine VaR and CVaR with excellent accuracy and a quadratic speedup relative to classical methods.
solution_approaches.location: Page 10, Section V.B. Risk analysis, paragraph 3

solution_approaches.approach: implementation of quantum risk analysis algorithm as a quantum circuit tested on IBM Q Experience
solution_approaches.description: Prototype implementation of the VaR/CVaR quantum algorithm on IBM’s quantum hardware for small examples.
solution_approaches.quote: The authors of Ref. [81] went as far as constructing an imple- mentation of their algorithm as a quantum score, which was tested for some small examples on the IBM Q Expe- rience.
solution_approaches.location: Page 10, Section V.B. Risk analysis, paragraph 3

problem_solution_mappings.approach: training neural networks using a quantum annealer
problem_solution_mappings.quote:
These properties have made neural networks essential for, e.g., ﬁnancial time-series prediction [74, 75]. There exist a number of proposals to accelerate neural networks and deep learn- ing algorithms through the power of quantum computing [76–78], which we will brieﬂy review in the following.
While machine learning algorithms are usually ex- tremely eﬃcient, their training can be computationally expensive. This overhead could be signiﬁcantly reduced by training the neural network using a quantum an- nealer, such as the D-Wave or the Rigetti machines.

In this situation, obtaining a quantum speedup could make a notable diﬀerence.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computation holds the promise of highly efficient algorithms providing exponential speedups for some technologically important problems relevant to finance.
key_claims.quote:
Relative to classical information processing, quantum
computation holds the promise of highly eﬃcient algo-
rithms, providing exponential speedups for some techno-
logically important problems [2].
key_claims.location: Page 1, Introduction

key_claims.claim: Many financial problems can be naturally formulated as optimization tasks that are particularly hard for classical computers but suitable for quantum optimization methods.
key_claims.quote:
Many problems in ﬁnance can be expressed as opti-
mization problems. These are tasks which are partic-
ularly hard for classical computers, but ﬁnd a natural
formulation using quantum optimization methods [7].
key_claims.location: Page 1–2, Introduction

key_claims.claim: Quantum annealers have already been successfully used in proof-of-principle experiments for practical financial problems and are expected to have practical value in the near future.
key_claims.quote:
Let us now focus on three case-examples where quan-
tum optimization has been used successfully in practi-
cal ﬁnancial problems. While these results are proof-
of-principles, they demonstrate that, in the near future,
quantum annealers will have practical value with regards
to problems in ﬁnance.
key_claims.location: Page 5, Section III Quantum Optimization

key_claims.claim: Quantum machine learning algorithms offer substantial speedups for key subroutines such as PCA, SVM, and Boltzmann machines, which are relevant to financial applications.
key_claims.quote:
A summary of speedups available for QML algorithms is
provided in Table III.
key_claims.location: Page 4, Section II.D The case for quantum computing in ﬁnance

key_claims.claim: Quantum PCA can reduce the cost of principal component analysis from quadratic in matrix size to polylogarithmic, vastly broadening its applicability in finance.
key_claims.quote:
It was recently shown that a version of this algorithm,
the quantum-PCA algorithm, could be run exponentially
faster on a quantum processor [22]. Speciﬁcally, this
algorithm ﬁnds approximations to the principal compo-
nents of a correlation matrix, with a computational cost
ofO((logN)2) (both in computational and query com-
plexities). This development should vastly broaden the
spectrum of applicability of PCA, allowing us to estimate
risk and maximize proﬁt in situations that were not fea-
sible using classical methods.
key_claims.location: Page 8, Section IV.C Principal component analysis

key_claims.claim: Quantum regression methods based on HHL can achieve exponential speedup over classical least-squares regression for suitable training matrices.
key_claims.quote:
They showed that, for a sparse
training data matrix, they could encode the model’s op-
timal ﬁt parameters into the amplitudes of a quantum
state. This can be done in a time which is exponentially
faster than the fastest classical algorithm [27].
key_claims.location: Page 8, Section IV.B Regression

key_claims.claim: Constructing a quantum computer that outperforms classical computers is extremely challenging due to decoherence, error correction overhead, and hardware limitations like qRAM.
key_claims.quote:
We caution the reader that constructing a quantum
computer which is capable of outperforming classical
computers is a truly formidable task, and potentially one
of the great challenges of the century. Before we reach
this level, a number of critical issues will have to be dealt
with.
key_claims.location: Page 4–5, Section II.F Challenges for quantum computing

key_claims.claim: Error correction overhead can negate the apparent speedup of quantum algorithms when classical processing for error correction is included.
key_claims.quote:
In a recent study,
it was estimated that quantum computing could achieve
a signiﬁcant speedup (in absolute time), but this advan-
tage vanished when the classical processing required to
implement error-correction schemes was taken into ac-
count [37].
key_claims.location: Page 5, Section II.F Challenges for quantum computing

key_claims.claim: Many promising quantum machine learning algorithms require universal quantum computers, which are more technologically challenging than current quantum annealers.
key_claims.quote:
Note that, while many QML algorithms are potentially
ground breaking, many of them require the operation of a
universal quantum computer. These are more advanced
than quantum annealers, and are also more technolog-
ically challenging.
key_claims.location: Page 7, Section IV Quantum Machine Learning

key_claims.claim: Even widely accepted financial models can fail in qualitatively new situations, and it remains unproven whether quantum computing can predict such events.
key_claims.quote:
While quantum com-
puting provides powerful computational tools, whether
or not it can predict this type of events remains to be
proven.
key_claims.location: Page 2, Introduction (cautionary note about 2008 crash)

key_claims.claim: Quantum annealing, even as an approximate realization of adiabatic computing, can find near-optimal solutions to NP-hard optimization problems in polynomial time.
key_claims.quote:
Quantum annealing is therefore
an approximate realization of adiabatic computing. It
was shown by Zagoskin that approximate adiabatic com-
puting can ﬁnd a solution which is close to optimal – a
problem which is also known to be NP-hard – in polyno-
mial time [47].
key_claims.location: Page 5, Section III Quantum Optimization

key_claims.claim: Current D-Wave quantum annealers can solve small instances of financial optimization problems with performance similar to classical hardware and high success rates.
key_claims.quote:
This problem was solved on two D-Wave chips with
512 and 1152 qubits [43]. While only small instances
were implemented, the performance of the quantum an-
nealers was similar to that of classical hardware. These
experiments proved that this problem can be solved on
the D-Wave machine with a high success rate.
key_claims.location: Page 6, Section III.A Optimal trading trajectory

key_claims.claim: Quantum annealers reproduced optimal arbitrage solutions found by exhaustive classical solvers in small examples.
key_claims.quote:
It was found that the quantum annealer pro-
duced the same optimal solutions as an exhaustive clas-
sical solver [49].
key_claims.location: Page 6, Section III.B Optimal arbitrage opportunities

key_claims.claim: NISQ algorithms are a promising near-term route to quantum supremacy but require development of a substantial algorithm library.
key_claims.quote:
In view of these obstacles, many researchers have
turned to algorithms for so called Noisy Intermediate-
Scale Quantum (NISQ) processors. ... Being an extremely new direction of
study, we lack an important algorithm library for NISQ
machines. This is another great software challenge: to
develop new algorithms to make near term quantum com-
puters applicable to real world problems.
key_claims.location: Page 5, Section II.F Challenges for quantum computing

key_claims.claim: The lack of a practical quantum RAM is one of the largest hardware challenges for applying quantum computing to data-intensive problems like those in finance.
key_claims.quote:
At present, we do not have a
quantum RAM (qRAM) capable of eﬃciently encoding
this information as a quantum state, and reliably storing
it for extended periods of time. This is among the largest
hardware challenges for quantum computing.
key_claims.location: Page 5, Section II.F Challenges for quantum computing

key_claims.claim: Neural networks are extremely successful in predicting markets and analyzing credit risk, and quantum computing can accelerate their training.
key_claims.quote: Neural networks have proved extremely successful at predicting markets and analyzing credit risk [72, 73]. ... There exist a number of proposals to accelerate neural networks and deep learn- ing algorithms through the power of quantum computing [76–78], which we will brieﬂy review in the following.
key_claims.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 1

key_claims.claim: Training neural networks on quantum annealers could be less prone to local minima than standard methods.
key_claims.quote: We expect this method to be less prone to falling into local minima than standard training methods (such a gradient descent, Hessian methods, backpropagation, stochastic gradient descent, ...).
key_claims.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 2

key_claims.claim: A Boltzmann machine can be efficiently trained using present day D-Wave quantum computers.
key_claims.quote: Ref. [79] have shown that a Boltzmann machine could be eﬃciently trained using present day D-Wave quantum computer.
key_claims.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 3

key_claims.claim: Montanaro’s quantum Monte Carlo algorithm achieves the same accuracy with almost quadratically fewer samples than classical Monte Carlo.
key_claims.quote: Montanaro showed that Monte Carlo simulations can run on a quantum com- puter, obtaining the same accuracy as predicted by Eq. (8) but with almost quadratically less samples k [10]. Speciﬁcally, Montanaro’s algorithm requires onlyO(σ/ϵ) samples (up to polylogarithmic factors) to estimate µ with 99% success probability.
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section V. QUANTUM AMPLITUDE ESTIMATION AND MONTE CARLO, paragraph after QAE description

key_claims.claim: Quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo can yield a quadratic speedup in pricing financial derivatives.
key_claims.quote: Rebentrost, Gupt, and Bromley suggested using quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo to obtain a quadratic speedup in pricing ﬁ- nancial derivatives [11].
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section V.A. Pricing of ﬁnancial derivatives, paragraph 2

key_claims.claim: Quantum risk analysis using QAE can determine VaR and CVaR with excellent accuracy and quadratic speedup relative to classical methods.
key_claims.quote: Speciﬁcally, by applying the QAE algorithm, which called a tailored oracle function, they were able to determine VaR and CVaR with excellent accuracy and a quadratic speedup relative to classical methods.
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section V.B. Risk analysis, paragraph 3

key_claims.claim: Small-size quantum experiments for risk analysis could already show a quantum speed-up relative to classical methods.
key_claims.quote: This is interesting because small-size experiments such as this one could already show a quantum speed-up relative to classical methods.
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section V.B. Risk analysis, paragraph 3

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing could disrupt finance and will likely play a key role in quantitative finance before long.
key_claims.quote: In this paper, we have reviewed ways in which quantum computing could disrupt ﬁnance. ... It is our belief that before long quantum computers will play a key role in quantitative ﬁnance.
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section VI. CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES, paragraph 1

key_claims.claim: Faulty (non–fault-tolerant) quantum computers may find interesting financial applications before fully universal fault-tolerant devices exist.
key_claims.quote: It is possible, however, that faulty quantum computers will ﬁnd inter- esting applications far before we achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing. We would expect it is in this area that the ﬁrst real disruptions to ﬁnance will occur, and urge researchers to investigate this fascinating direction of study.
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section VI. CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES, paragraph 2

key_claims.claim: Quantum neural network ideas such as quantum perceptrons and quantum hidden Markov models are still in their infancy and need further study.
key_claims.quote: While promising, these ideas are still very much in their infancy, and need to be further studied before their power is fully understood.
key_claims.location: Page 9, Section D. Neural networks and associated models, paragraph 7

key_claims.claim: Several potentially important applications of quantum physics in the economy, such as blockchain, quantum money, and quantum cryptography for financial transactions, are not covered and remain for future work.
key_claims.quote: There are a number of applications that quantum physics ﬁnds in economy that, while fascinating, we chose not to cover. It would have been interesting to talk about how quantum technologies can be relevant to the blockchain and cryptocurrencies [82], or to discuss quan- tum ﬁnance [5, 6], quantum money [83], the impact of quantum cryptography in the security of ﬁnancial trans- actions [15, 84], and the applications of quantum sim- ulators [85, 86] in ﬁnance. These could constitute an interesting subject for a future publication.
key_claims.location: Page 10, Section VI. CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES, paragraph 3
